title: Technology and Its Costs
theme: Technology and society: convenience, privacy and consent
objectives: I can use ten words to describe how technology changes privacy, work, and information.
I can explain the difference between watching for safety and surveillance, and between privacy and secrecy.
I can explain what makes consent real and what makes a source anonymous.
I can write a balanced paragraph about a technology decision using at least four words from this unit.
rationale: Students live inside the debates this unit names, so eighth grade is the right place to give them exact words for them. The ten words cover what technology does (automate, algorithm, proliferate, virtual, artificial), what it can cost people (privacy, surveillance, misinformation), and what a fair process requires (consent, anonymous). Consent is taught with its verb sense beside the noun, and misinformation with the neighbor word disinformation in the teacher note. The unit pulls ethics, credibility and manipulation from earlier units into one practical case that asks whether a school should adopt a technology, not just whether it works.

words.def: To make a process run on machines or computers with little human effort.
words.ex: The bakery decided to automate its ordering, so computers now track the supply of flour and sugar.
words.ex2: Engineers have found ways to automate jobs that once took workers hours, such as sorting packages.
words.nonExample: A cook who stirs soup by hand all afternoon has not automated anything.

apps.academic: Economists study how efforts to automate jobs change which skills workers need.
apps.spoken: I wish we could automate cleaning my room.
apps.writing: Say what is being automated and who gains or loses, because to automate a job is rarely a neutral choice.

cloze.s: To save time, the library will ___ its checkout, so that scanners and computers do the work clerks once did by hand.

cloze2.s: The factory chose to ___ the assembly line, replacing repetitive hand tasks with robotic arms.

misuse.s: To automate the lunch line, the school hired twelve more people to write down every order by hand.
misuse.why: To automate is to let machines do the work; hiring people to write orders by hand is the opposite.

visual.alt: A robot arm beside a large gear.

words.frame: I would automate ___ because ___, but I would worry about ___.

words.def: The freedom to keep your personal information, activities, and space away from the view or control of others.
words.ex: Students have a reasonable expectation of privacy in the school's changing rooms.
words.ex2: Before downloading the app, Mia read how it protected her privacy and which data it shared.
words.nonExample: A photo you post for the whole internet to see keeps very little privacy.

apps.academic: Laws about privacy limit how companies and governments may collect and use personal data.
apps.spoken: Please respect my privacy and knock before you come in.
apps.writing: Say whose privacy and from whom, since privacy from a friend is different from privacy from a company.

cloze.s: She locked her journal in a drawer because she believed her diary entries deserved ___.

cloze2.s: The new law protects the ___ of patients by limiting who may read their medical records.

misuse.s: The students enjoyed complete privacy because every message they sent was posted for the whole school to read.
misuse.why: Privacy is keeping information to yourself; posting messages for everyone destroys it.

visual.alt: A closed door secured with a padlock.

words.def: Close, continuing watch over people or places, often by cameras or computers, to collect information.
words.ex: Cameras above the entrance provided constant surveillance of the parking lot.
words.ex2: Critics worry that widespread surveillance makes people afraid to speak freely.
words.nonExample: Glancing at a classmate's quiz is not surveillance, because surveillance is ongoing and organized watching.
words.rel: watching people on a continuing basis

apps.academic: Debates about surveillance weigh public safety against individual freedom.
apps.spoken: I do not love being under surveillance every time I walk through the mall.
apps.writing: Name who is watching and why, since a parent, a store, and a government use surveillance very differently.

cloze.s: The government's ___ of its citizens included reading their messages and tracking their phones every day.

cloze2.s: The store's camera ___ helped catch the thief, but some customers felt watched while they shopped.

misuse.s: The surveillance of the park lasted one second, when a girl briefly glanced at a pigeon.
misuse.why: Surveillance is close, continuing, organized watching; a single glance is not.

visual.alt: A security camera above a large open eye.

words.frame: Surveillance may be justified when ___ but not when ___.

words.def: A set of step-by-step rules that a computer follows to solve a problem or make a decision.
words.ex: The video app's algorithm picks the next clip by studying what you have already watched.
words.ex2: A simple algorithm for sorting names puts them in alphabetical order by comparing two names at a time.
words.nonExample: A single guess, with no steps or rules behind it, is not an algorithm.

apps.academic: In mathematics and computer science, an algorithm lists exact steps that lead to an answer.
apps.spoken: The algorithm keeps showing me videos about skateboarding.
apps.writing: Say what the algorithm is trying to do, since its goal shapes what it notices and what it ignores.

cloze.s: Each time you finish a song, the music app's ___ uses your listening history to choose what plays next.

cloze2.s: To split the class into fair teams, Ravi wrote an ___ with clear steps that anyone could follow.

misuse.s: The algorithm was a random wave of the hand that the computer made up as it went along, with no rules at all.
misuse.why: An algorithm is a set of clear step-by-step rules, not a random act.

visual.alt: Boxes joined by arrows that show a series of steps leading to a decision.

words.def: Made by people rather than occurring in nature; not genuine.
words.ex: The artificial flowers on the table looked real until she touched the plastic petals.
words.ex2: The company added artificial sweeteners to its drink to cut the sugar.
words.nonExample: A tree growing in a forest is natural, not artificial.
words.rel: made by people, not by nature

apps.academic: In computing, artificial intelligence means software built to do tasks that usually require human thinking.
apps.spoken: I can taste that the flavor is artificial.
apps.writing: Artificial can sound negative, so choose synthetic or man-made when you want a neutral tone.

cloze.s: The ___ lake in the middle of the park was dug by workers and filled with water from a pipe.

cloze2.s: Because the food coloring was ___, it came from a laboratory rather than from fruit or vegetables.

misuse.s: The artificial lake formed naturally over thousands of years as a glacier melted.
misuse.why: Artificial means made by people; a lake formed by a melting glacier is natural.

visual.alt: A real flower beside a robot.

words.def: False or misleading information that spreads, whether or not the person sharing it knows it is wrong.
words.ex: Misinformation about the storm spread quickly after someone posted an old video as if it were new.
words.ex2: The librarian taught students to check three sources before sharing a surprising claim, so they would not pass along misinformation.
words.nonExample: An accurate news report that carries a clearly labeled correction is not misinformation.

segs.m: facts or knowledge that is passed along

apps.academic: Researchers study how misinformation spreads and what slows it down.
apps.spoken: Check it before you share it, because it might be misinformation.
apps.writing: Separate misinformation, which can be shared by mistake, from disinformation, which is spread on purpose.

cloze.s: The post claiming school was canceled for a week was ___, and the principal had to correct it.

cloze2.s: Fact-checkers worked all night to correct the ___ that had spread about the date of the election.

misuse.s: The teacher praised the report as full of misinformation, because every statement had been checked and proven true.
misuse.why: Misinformation is false or misleading; statements that were checked and proven true are the opposite.

visual.alt: A phone showing a large question mark.

words.frame: I can slow the spread of misinformation by ___.

words.def: To increase quickly in number and spread widely.
words.ex: After the video went viral, copies of it began to proliferate across the internet.
words.ex2: Weeds proliferate in a garden that no one tends during a rainy summer.
words.nonExample: A population that stays the same size year after year is not proliferating.

apps.academic: Biologists describe how cells proliferate, and media researchers describe how rumors proliferate.
apps.spoken: Coffee shops have proliferated on our street.
apps.writing: Use proliferate for a fast increase in number, not for growth in size.

cloze.s: Once the app became popular, copycat versions began to ___ in the store, until there were hundreds of them.

cloze2.s: Bacteria can ___ in warm, moist conditions, doubling in number in a short time.

misuse.s: Rumors proliferate when only one person hears them and no one ever repeats them.
misuse.why: To proliferate is to multiply quickly; a rumor that no one repeats does not spread at all.

visual.alt: Tiny germs multiplying, with a plus sign beside them.

words.def: Existing or taking place on a computer or online rather than in the physical world.
words.ex: The class took a virtual field trip to the museum, exploring its galleries on a screen.
words.ex2: Because of the snowstorm, the committee held a virtual meeting instead of gathering in the library.
words.nonExample: A real basketball game played in a gym is not a virtual one.
words.rel: on a screen instead of in person

apps.academic: Virtual models let scientists test ideas on a computer before they build anything.
apps.spoken: We had a virtual birthday party over video.
apps.writing: Say what is virtual, since a virtual meeting, a virtual tour, and a virtual currency each mean something different.

cloze.s: Since the storm closed the roads, the students joined the ___ meeting from their kitchens and bedrooms.

cloze2.s: The architect walked through a ___ model of the building on her laptop before a single wall was built.

misuse.s: The virtual museum tour required everyone to ride a bus and walk through the real galleries.
misuse.why: A virtual tour happens on a screen; riding a bus to walk the real galleries is a physical trip.

words.frame: A virtual version of ___ is useful because ___.

words.def: Permission freely given by someone who understands what they are agreeing to.

senses.example: After reading the rules, the parents consented to the trip.

words.ex: The hospital cannot treat a child without the consent of a parent or guardian.
words.ex2: Many privacy laws require a company to ask for your consent before it collects certain personal data.
words.nonExample: Staying silent because you feel pressured is not real consent.

apps.academic: Informed consent means a person understands the risks of a study before agreeing to join it.
apps.spoken: Ask for consent before you post someone else's picture.
apps.writing: A full sentence about consent says who gives it, to what, and with what information.

cloze.s: Before the study began, each volunteer signed a form giving ___ to be interviewed, after the risks had been explained.

cloze2.s: Posting a classmate's photo online without her ___ can be unfair, even if you meant it as a joke.

misuse.s: The company claimed it had her consent even though she had never seen the settings and had never been asked.
misuse.why: Consent must be freely given by someone who knows what they are agreeing to; she was never asked.

visual.alt: A hand signing a form with a check mark.

words.def: Not named or identified; the name of the person is kept unknown.
words.ex: The anonymous survey let students answer honestly without writing their names.
words.ex2: An anonymous donor paid for the new playground and asked that no plaque be put up.
words.nonExample: A letter signed with the writer's full name is not anonymous.

apps.academic: Researchers often keep survey answers anonymous so that participants feel free to be honest.
apps.spoken: The tip was anonymous, so we do not know who sent it.
apps.writing: Separate anonymous (no one knows the name) from confidential (someone knows but will not tell).

cloze.s: The ___ note on the teacher's desk praised the class, but no one could tell who had written it.

cloze2.s: To protect the volunteers, the report kept every interview ___ and used numbers instead of names.

misuse.s: The anonymous author signed her full name at the top of every page and added her home address.
misuse.why: Anonymous means the name is unknown; signing a full name and address is the opposite.

visual.alt: A theater mask above a question mark.

words.frame: An anonymous report is useful when ___ but risky when ___.

passage.title: The Hallway Tracker
paras: Last spring, the principal at Ridgeview Middle School proposed a plan to automate attendance. Instead of teachers calling names, cameras in the hallways would feed an algorithm that matched each student's face to a photo on file. The principal said the system would save ten minutes a day and make the building safer.

At the first student council meeting, opinions split. Dana liked the idea of artificial intelligence doing boring paperwork. Theo pointed out that no one had asked students for their consent, and that cameras recording every hallway looked less like attendance and more like surveillance. “It is not that I have something to hide,” he said. “It is that my privacy should not end at the classroom door.”

Meanwhile, rumors began to proliferate online. One post claimed that the cameras would send students' photos to advertisers. Another said they would be used to lower grades. Neither claim named a source. Misinformation, the council's adviser reminded them, spreads fastest when people are anxious and no one has explained what is really happening.

To learn what students actually thought, the council ran an anonymous survey, so that no one would fear punishment for an honest answer. They also invited the principal to a virtual town hall, where families who could not come to the building could ask questions by video.

The results surprised everyone. Most students were not against automation itself, but eighty-one percent wanted to know who could see the data and how long it would be stored. The principal agreed to pause the plan until the district could answer those questions in writing. Dana still liked the technology, and Theo still doubted it. But both agreed that the question was no longer whether the system could work. It was whether the school should use it, and on whose terms.

qs.q: In paragraph 3, the word “proliferate” most nearly means
choices: disappear from view
increase quickly in number
become more accurate
be deleted by teachers
qs.why: The rumors multiply across the internet, each post spreading a new claim, so the word means to increase quickly in number.

qs.q: Why does Theo say the cameras look “less like attendance and more like surveillance”?
choices: They would be too expensive for a school budget.
They would be installed by the students themselves.
They would watch every hallway continuously, not only record who is present.
They would be unable to recognize any faces.
qs.why: Attendance needs only a list of who is present, but cameras recording all hallways collect far more information through continuing watch.

qs.q: Which detail best shows that the survey was designed to encourage honest answers?
choices: It was anonymous, so students did not fear punishment.
Students were asked to sign their names.
The principal ran the survey in person.
Only council members could answer it.
qs.why: The passage says the council ran an anonymous survey so that no one would fear punishment for an honest answer.

qs.q: What is the most likely reason the principal agrees to pause the plan?
choices: The cameras stopped working during the survey.
Dana withdrew her support for the technology.
The district banned all technology in schools.
The survey showed students wanted clear answers about who could see the data and how long it would be stored.
qs.why: Eighty-one percent of students wanted those questions answered, and the principal agrees to pause until the district answers them in writing.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses a central idea of the passage?
choices: Cameras in schools always cause rumors.
Whether a technology works is only part of the question; whether and how it should be used also matters.
Students should never be asked their opinions about technology.
Artificial intelligence is too difficult for schools to understand.
qs.why: The final paragraph says the question is no longer whether the system could work, but whether the school should use it and on whose terms.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words for thinking about technology as an ethical issue, not only a convenience. They practice distinguishing privacy from secrecy, surveillance from safety, and misinformation from disinformation, and they read a narrative in which a student council weighs a school camera plan. The unit draws on the earlier units on ethics, credibility and manipulation, and it supports the argument writing that follows.

notes.va.automate.v: Automate is the neutral, concrete entry point. Ask what jobs in the community have been automated and what changed for workers. Students may confuse automate with automatic: an automatic device acts by itself, and to automate is to make a process work that way.
notes.va.privacy.n: Privacy is not the same as secrecy: someone can keep a diary private without having anything to hide. Ask students to name three things they keep private and from whom. Avoid asking students to disclose personal information in class.
notes.va.surveillance.n: Surveillance is organized and continuing watching. It is not always sinister: a lifeguard's watch is one kind. Have students sort scenarios by who watches, why, and whether the person knows. Stress that the noun, not the verb, is the target here.
notes.va.algorithm.n: Algorithm is a tier 3 term kept concrete: a recipe is a good analogy. Ask students for an algorithm for making a sandwich, then ask what happens if a step is vague. Connect to how apps choose what to show, and note that the rules reflect choices made by people.
notes.va.artificial.adj: Artificial means made by people. It does not always mean fake or bad: an artificial lake is real water. Link to the phrase artificial intelligence and ask what is made by people and what it is meant to imitate.
notes.va.misinformation.n: Misinformation is false information, shared knowingly or not. Disinformation is false information spread on purpose; give students both words so they can name intent. Note the prefix mis- (wrongly) added to information. Practice a three-step check before sharing.
notes.va.proliferate.v: Proliferate means increase quickly in number. It applies to cells, weeds, apps, and rumors, but not to growth in size. Ask students for something that proliferated in their lives, such as videos or snack brands.
notes.va.virtual.adj: Virtual means on a screen or computer rather than in physical space. Students may know the everyday adverb virtually (almost); mention it only if it comes up. Compare virtual and physical versions of a meeting, a tour, and a game.
notes.va.consent.n: Consent is free, informed permission. Teach the three tests: freely given, informed, and able to be taken back. The verb sense appears as a second sense. Be careful and age-appropriate; keep examples about photos, data and school activities.
notes.va.anonymous.adj: Anonymous means the name is unknown. Contrast with confidential (someone knows but will not tell). Ask when anonymity helps (honest surveys, tips) and when it hurts (harassment). Use examples carefully.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: “The plan is to automate attendance with an algorithm and cameras. The principal says it saves time, and that may be true. But I have to ask who gave consent, who can see the data, and whether continuous watching is surveillance rather than attendance. The anonymous survey is useful because students can say what they think without fear.”
discuss: When is it fair for a school or a company to watch people, and what limits should apply?
Does an algorithm make a decision fairer, or just faster? Who chooses its rules?
How can you tell whether a post is misinformation before you share it?
misconceptions: Privacy means having something to hide.
Anonymous and confidential mean the same thing.
Artificial always means fake or bad.
An algorithm is a computer's opinion.
extend: Write a one-page policy proposal for how your school should handle a technology that collects data, including consent, access and storage time.
Track a viral claim to its original source and report what you find, using at least four words from the unit.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Bring back ethics, accountable, credibility and manipulate when students analyze the principal's plan and the online rumors. Revisit consent and anonymous after two days with new scenarios, and use surveillance and proliferate in the consequences unit at the end of the year.

needsReview: Spanish glosses not reviewed by a native speaker: vigilancia (surveillance), desinformación (covers both misinformation and disinformation), privacidad, consentimiento, automatizar, proliferar.
Sense boundaries: consent taught as a noun with the verb as a second sense; surveillance and virtual are intentionally limited to their core senses (virtually is not taught).
Facts to confirm: many privacy laws require a company to ask for consent before collecting certain data (general statement, no specific law named).
Morphology: misinformation segmented as mis- plus information only; automate is not segmented because no etymology is claimed.
